transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

I feel like no matter how hard I plan and work, I’m just not good enough to get ahead. Lately, I've just been feeling so stuck and unmotivated with my career and my goals, and it feels like nothing I do really matters anymore.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in most activities you used to enjoy, even things like hobbies, socializing, or spending time with loved ones?

Yeah, I really have. Things I used to love, like my neighborhood clean-ups and working on my financial plans, just don't feel meaningful to me anymore. I've even started canceling plans and turning down friends and neighbors because I'm just too tired and unmotivated to show up.
How long have you been feeling this way? Was there a specific event that started these feelings, or has it been building over time?

I’ve been feeling this way for about three years now, starting right after I was passed over for a supervisor promotion in favor of a younger, less-experienced coworker. At the exact same time, budget cuts at my company increased my workload, leaving me feeling completely overwhelmed and unappreciated.
Have you had any periods lasting at least several weeks in the past three years where your mood improved and you felt significantly better or back to normal, even for a short time?

No, I haven't had any breaks from this at all. Ever since I missed out on that promotion, this heavy, discouraged feeling has just been my constant baseline. I haven't had even a couple of weeks where I felt like my normal self or felt any real relief.
Have you had any previous episodes of depression before this three-year period, where you felt persistently low and lost interest in activities?

No, I don't recall ever having any similar episodes of feeling this low or losing interest before that time. Before those three years ago, I was generally pretty motivated and active with my projects.

The patient reports a persistent low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, fatigue, and feelings of worthlessness lasting for approximately three years, with onset linked to a psychosocial stressor (being passed over for promotion and increased workload). These symptoms meet criteria for a depressive episode. The chronicity of symptoms—lasting over two years—could suggest either a persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), which under ICD-10 falls under F34.1 (Persistent mood [affective] disorder), but given that the current presentation meets full criteria for a depressive episode of at least two years' duration, it may also qualify as a chronic form of depression within F32 (depressive episode) or support a diagnosis of recurrent depressive disorder F33 if there have been multiple episodes. However, the patient describes a continuous course since one triggering event without clear remission, which makes F34.1 a possible consideration. Yet, because the symptom severity includes marked functional impairment and meets full threshold for a depressive episode, F32 (for a current episode) remains appropriate. F33 is still considered if there is history of prior episodes, though not yet confirmed. Thus, the differential remains between F32 (for current major depressive episode) and F33 (if recurrence is established later). No new information excludes either, so candidates remain unchanged.

The onset was linked to psychosocial stressors including workplace injustice and increased workload, with no prior depressive episodes reported.
